body:
V15

> Many ASVS requirements either relate to a particular area of security like authentication or authorization or relate to a particular type of application functionality such as logging or file handling.

Proposal:
> Many ASVS requirements either relate to a particular area of security, such as authentication or authorization, or relate to a particular type of application functionality, such as logging or file handling.

---

> However, this chapter provides more general guidance on how to build applications and how to write secure code correctly. Not just from the perspective of clean architecture and code quality, but rather specific architecture and coding practices that need to be followed in order for the application to be secure.

The 2nd sentence helps to clarify it, but if to watch the first sentence separately:
* "how to build" may be associated with a build pipeline as a process, should be reworded to the meaning "architecture"
* "how to write secure code correctly" - "how to write" may be nowadays translated to "which AI IDE to use"

---

> This chapter also contains requirements to prevent the introduction of malicious code into the application.

Outdated leftover?

---

V15.1 Secure Coding Documentation

> Many of the requirements needed for a secure and defendable architecture require having clear documentation around what components are used in the application.

I want to highlight, that we need clear security decisions, that need to be documented.
> Many of the requirements needed for a secure and defendable architecture require having clear documented security decisions around what components are used in the application.

The same applies for this, and it needs some more commas as well:
> This section provides the requirements for this documentation including which of these components are risky due to being poorly maintained, unsupported, end of life, or with a history of significant vulnerabilities and which components perform risky operations such as deserialization of untrusted data, raw file parsing or direct memory manipulation. It also includes mandates defining appropriate timescales for addressing vulnerabilities in 3rd party components.

---

V15.2 Security Architecture and Dependencies

> This section includes requirements for handling risky, outdated or insecure dependencies and components through dependency management. It also includes using architectural level techniques such as sandboxing, encapsulation, containerization, and network isolation to reduce the impact of risky operations or libaries and preventing loss of availability due to overusing resource-demanding functionality.


Typofix and grammar:
> This section includes requirements for handling risky, outdated, or insecure dependencies and components through dependency management. It also includes using architectural-level techniques such as sandboxing, encapsulation, containerization, and network isolation to reduce the impact of risky operations or libraries and prevent loss of availability due to overusing resource-demanding functionality.

---

V15.3 Defensive Coding

> This section covers vulnerability types including type juggling, prototype pollution, mass assignment, and others which result from the use of insecure coding patterns in a particular language. Some may not be relevant to all languages whereas others will have language specific fixes or may relate to the way that a particular language or framework handles a feature such as HTTP parameters. It also considers the risk of not cryptographically validating application updates.

Grammar:
> This section covers vulnerability types, including type juggling, prototype pollution, mass assignment, and others, which result from the use of insecure coding patterns in a particular language. Some may not be relevant to all languages, whereas others will have language-specific fixes or may relate to the way that a particular language or framework handles a feature such as HTTP parameters. It also considers the risk of not cryptographically validating application updates.

comments.body:
> "how to write secure code correctly" - "how to write" may be nowadays translated to "which AI IDE to use"

Not sure what you are proposing.

For everything else, I opened #2975

"this chapter provides more general guidance on how to develop secure applications and how to write secure code correctly"

If to read it really literally, we don't describe HOW to develop or HOW to write, we have requirements for verifying the result. "HOW TO" describes the process to achieve that and that is out of scope.
Well we have requirements to be taken in to account whilst building, no?
Discussed with Elar to use: "However, this chapter provides more general security requirements to be taken into account when designing and developing applications."

> Discussed with Elar to use: "However, this chapter provides more general security requirements to be taken into account when designing and developing applications."

Opened #2978

> "this chapter provides more general guidance on how to develop secure applications and how to write secure code correctly"
> 
> If to read it really literally, we don't describe HOW to develop or HOW to write, we have requirements for verifying the result. "HOW TO" describes the process to achieve that and that is out of scope.

I would agree that most developer guidance on how to develop secure applications and how to write secure code correctly has been removed. This standard is not very actionable by developers anymore. But I do admit it's a great deal more focused on and better for security testers.

> I would agree that most developer guidance on how to develop secure applications and how to write secure code correctly has been removed.

This is something I fully disagree. First, we never had requirements on how developer needs to write the code, requirements for development environment etc.

And second, I have developer background and try to keep this in mind, my main focus can be nowadays from verification perspective, but @tghosth  is "fighting" for developers perspective all the time. It should be acknowledged, we are not duplicating the Cheat Sheet series or testing guide project.

> This standard is not very actionable by developers anymore.

For clarifying the requirement, being actionable has taken quite some time and effort from me. If you come with such claims, be ready to back them up with precise examples with the intent to improve them.

Such claims, first, are not true, and second, do not help anyone here. And in any other places.

Elar, I was just trying to echo a comment you made earlier. 

> If to read it really literally, we don't describe HOW to develop or HOW to write, we have requirements for verifying the result. "HOW TO" describes the process to achieve that and that is out of scope.

I feel the direction of ASVS is a lot more actionable for testers and less so for developers. So many of the code quality and engineering requirements have gone away to recommendations section. This is not an attack on you or Josh -  its just my perspective. When working with developers, which is my life's work, we need to be very specific at the code level, and most of ASVS has removed my and others earlier attempts to add that in. What we have now is more of a testing standard, less of a developer one. And that is not all an attack on you, it's a concern and perspective from me, echoed from your own comments.

Did I miss something? I am open to you feedback on this.

PS: I moved my concerns about developers here as a more appropriate place to discuss this.

https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2983
I think we have taken this discussion elsewhere so I will close this for now. If I have misunderstood, feel free to reopen
